title: Liquid-Cooling Leak-Test Crews for AI Data Centers
one_liner: A specialty crew of journeyman plumbers that flushes, fills, pressure-tests and photo-documents every quick-disconnect in AI liquid-cooled halls, sold per rack to neoclouds and the contractors building for them.
customer: Neocloud and colocation operators building liquid-cooled GPU halls, and the mechanical and general contractors on those builds who carry the commissioning schedule and the liability.
problem: Liquid cooling for AI racks turns data centers into plumbing systems with hundreds of quick-disconnect pairs per rack and coolant loops feeding hardware worth millions. Leaks at quick disconnects were among the failures during the first field ramps of dense racks. Commissioning delays on a large hall cost on the order of $14M per month, and pipefitters and mechanical trades are named in July 2026 surveys as one of the top three labor gaps. Much of the rack-level wet work is done by data-center technicians and electricians who were never trained in flushing, air removal, test discipline or cleanliness, so tests pass on Friday and a fitting drips on Monday.
solution: A three-person 'wet-work pod' (two journeymen and one apprentice) with a kit: pressure-decay test rig at 1.5x operating pressure, a filtered flush cart with a particle counter, a glycol refractometer, a borescope, UV dye and torque tools. The pod flushes and fills loops, purges air, tests and re-tests, and logs every quick-disconnect with a photo, QR tag and rack serial, generating the traceable leak-test record the lender, the insurer and the operator want. Priced per rack or per pod-day, with a commissioning-window guarantee. Later add a warranty-backed re-inspection after thermal cycling.
why_now: Liquid cooling roughly doubled in 2025 and is forecast to keep compounding, the racks in the field have far higher density and leak sensitivity than air-cooled halls, and the labor gap in pipefitting is the acknowledged constraint. Operators are paying premiums for anyone with liquid-loop experience, and the cost of one leaked rack dwarfs the cost of the crew.
revenue_model: $350-900 per rack for flush, fill, test and documented verification, or $2,400-3,500 per pod-day with a minimum engagement, plus paid re-inspection visits and a documentation package fee. Gross margin of 30-40% after paying journeymen $75-95 per hour, well above residential wages.
non_obvious_insight: Data center people think the hard part is the chip; plumbers know the hard part is water. Air pockets, thermal expansion, dirty new pipe (flux, cutting oil, thread dope), dissimilar metals and untested O-rings are what leak, and a documented test is worth more than a passed one. For a plumbing shop this is also a retention weapon: a road crew at data center rates keeps a 35-year-old journeyman from leaving the trade.
first_30_days: Use permit filings to find three data center builds within driving distance and call the mechanical superintendents. Offer a paid two-day leak-test audit on one row of racks. In parallel finish subcontractor prequalification (OSHA 30, insurance, NDA, background checks) and build the QR-tag and photo log. Put two journeymen from the shop on a rotating schedule so the residential business does not suffer.

title: Refundable-Deposit Demand Proof for Indie Hardware
one_liner: A hosted reservation page that lets small hardware creators collect refundable $20-$50 deposits at tiered locked prices, giving them price-elasticity data and a demand certificate before they commit to a campaign or a factory MOQ.
customer: First- and second-time hardware and game creators planning a Kickstarter or Indiegogo launch, plus the small factories and pledge-manager agencies that advise them. Payer is the creator.
problem: Kickstarter median funding is $7,060 versus a $64,567 average, and Indiegogo's top performers all 'arrived with an audience already built.' Small creators have followers but no proof anyone will pay, so they either launch blind or over-order inventory.
solution: A Stripe Connect-based landing page where each deposit charges the creator's own account (no funds held by us) and is refunded on request. Visitors choose among three locked-in price tiers (A/B-testing price), and a referral queue rewards sharing. The dashboard shows deposit count by country, price-tier elasticity and expected launch-day conversion. A 'demand certificate' PDF can be handed to factories negotiating MOQ or to lenders offering inventory financing. Deposits convert with one click to day-one pledges on launch.
why_now: Big brands proved the pattern in 2025-26. eufyMake ran a $50 deposit to lock a $1,499 price before its April 2025 Kickstarter and raised over $10M in 14 hours. Creality's refundable $50 deposit unlocked a $649 VIP price for its filament maker, and the goal was hit in about 16.5 minutes. Meanwhile Indiegogo retired Flexible Funding in October 2025, so both platforms are all-or-nothing and the cost of launching without proof is higher.
revenue_model: $299 setup plus 1.5% of deposits processed, a $999 launch-readiness package (demand certificate, pricing test, launch-day email sequence), and $49/mo for post-launch late-pledge and pre-order pages.
non_obvious_insight: The most successful launches of 2025-26 did not start on Kickstarter. They started with money-backed waitlists. eufyMake opened a $50 deposit pre-order scheme to lock a $1,499 price ahead of the April 29 Kickstarter (https://www.notebookcheck.net/Anker-EufyMake-E1-UV-printer-Pre-order-deposit-scheme-now-open.999622.0.html) and then raised $46.76M from 17,822 backers (https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/3d-printer-breaks-kickstarter-record-raises-44m/493857). Creality took $50 refundable deposits for VIP $649 pricing on the M1 (https://makers101.com/creality-filament-maker-m1-shredder-r1-live-tracker/). Kickstarter's own pre-launch page only collects follows, and the ecosystem is top-heavy (median $7,060 vs average $64,567, and 'all Indiegogo top performers arrived with an audience', https://www.tcf.team/blog/q1-2026-crowdfunding-report). A deposit is a far stronger demand signal than a follower, and small creators have no tool to run one, no way to test three price points, and no artefact factories will trust.
first_30_days: Build the landing page and Stripe Connect flow in 2 weeks. Pitch 10 creators with live 'coming soon' pages on Kickstarter, offering a free pilot in exchange for a case study. Run a $20-$50 deposit test with one creator (target 150+ deposits) and document the elasticity result. Publish the case study on r/Kickstarter, BackerKit-focused groups and crowdfunding Discords, then charge the next 5 creators.

title: Outfall Guardian for Data-Center Construction Sites
one_liner: Continuous outfall monitoring, rapid pathogen testing and auto-generated permit paperwork for contractors building data-center campuses and fabs.
customer: General contractors, owner's representatives and developers building $1B+ data-center and semiconductor campuses. Multi-million-dollar schedule risk gives them a real budget, and the contractor or owner pays.
problem: Cheyenne revoked Meta's discharge permit after a rare bacterium in its wastewater was traced to a construction site, and Ohio scrapped a general permit after more than 7,000 comments. Water quality, not just quantity, is now a siting risk. Contractors treat water as volume and have no biology or continuous-monitoring capability during dewatering, stormwater and hydrostatic testing.
solution: Off-the-shelf multiparameter sensors (turbidity, pH, conductivity, temperature) at each outfall, weekly rapid qPCR pathogen and bacterial testing through a partner lab, automated discharge-monitoring reports and a time-stamped 'permit defense file' that shows compliance before regulators ask. Add a community-facing dashboard.
why_now: Moratoria, permit revocations and public comment fights make regulators and neighbors ask for data. Capex on campuses has exploded, and delay costs are large.
revenue_model: $3-8k/site/month plus per-test lab fees and onboarding fees.
non_obvious_insight: The construction phase is the unmonitored weak link in a water-quality chain everyone else audits. Third-party telemetry works like insurance-grade evidence, and the buyer's motive is schedule protection, not sustainability.
first_30_days: Publish an analysis of the Cheyenne case as top-of-funnel. Contact 10 contractors and owner's reps active in Northern Virginia, Ohio, Texas, Wyoming and Arizona. Pilot at one site with commercial sensors and a contract lab, and offer the first month free in exchange for a case study.

title: Keep-the-Laptop Severance With Certified Data Wipe
one_liner: At layoff time, employers offer departing remote workers the option to keep their own laptop, remotely wiped and reimaged with a certificate of erasure. The service recovers, refurbishes and resells the devices people don't keep.
customer: People Ops, IT and Finance leaders at companies running frequent small layoffs of remote and hybrid staff (roughly 10-500 people per round). They buy per device, often through outplacement firms and layoff counsel. The laid-off worker is the beneficiary.
problem: The 2026 labor market is low-fire, low-hire, so layoffs are frequent and small, and AI is the most-cited reason in Challenger data for five straight months. ITAD firms want pallets, not 40 laptops scattered across 40 homes. Unreturned devices are write-offs and data-exposure risks. Laid-off workers lose their tools just as they must freelance or job-hunt. Candidates are also increasingly expected to own capable hardware and AI tooling.
solution: On notice day the employee picks Keep or Return. Keep: the device is remotely wiped through the employer's MDM, reimaged clean with an open-source starter kit and optional AI-tool credits, and transferred at appraised fair value, which the employer can subsidize to zero (tax treatment confirmed with counsel). Return: prepaid box, chain-of-custody, refurbish and resell. The employer gets an asset-disposal record, a certificate of data erasure, and a reuse and Scope 3 report. Device-offboarding logistics vendors exist, but they sell shipping. None sells a keep-it option priced as severance.
why_now: DRAM prices are up about 400% since 2024, so even 3-year-old laptops carry real resale value. Amazon's January 2026 cut of about 16,000 corporate roles and AI-attributed cuts are normalizing rolling layoffs. Breaches such as the Mercor contractor data leak make loose devices a board-level concern. Employers face growing pressure to show soft-landing and circular-IT practices.
revenue_model: $40-90 per device fee from the employer. Resale margin on returned devices. Upsell of refurbished, warrantied laptop leases to laid-off freelancers. Referral fees from outplacement partners.
non_obvious_insight: The laptop is the one severance item worth much more to the employee than it costs the employer. It also removes the employer's biggest post-layoff liability, the unreturned device. Small, frequent AI-era layoffs create a long tail of single devices that the pallet-based ITAD industry ignores.
first_30_days: Pitch five HR and IT leaders through outplacement firms and employment-law contacts. Build the flow on existing MDM scripts (Jamf, Intune, Kandji) with a partner ITAD firm issuing certificates. Run a free pilot on one 50-person layoff, then charge about $60 per device. Publish the pilot's unreturned-device rate and cost per device as the case study.

title: FTC Review-Rule Audits for Franchisors
one_liner: Fixed-fee audits that find review gating, incentivised reviews and insider reviews across a franchisor's or dealer group's locations, and in the reputation vendors doing it for them.
customer: General counsel and marketing VPs at franchisors and multi-location operators (auto dealer groups, dental support organisations, home-services and fitness franchises), with reputation-management agencies as channel partners.
problem: The FTC Consumer Review Rule bans review gating, sentiment-conditional incentives, suppression and undisclosed insider reviews, with civil penalties of up to $53,088 per violation. The FTC sent 10 warning letters in Dec 2025 and obtained a $4M order (partly suspended) in July 2026. Local operators often use review-request software that quietly routes unhappy customers away from public sites, and franchisors are exposed to franchisee behaviour.
solution: A 'Rule Ready' audit. Scan Google, Yelp, Facebook and vertical sites across all locations for suspicious bursts, employee reviews and incentive language. Mystery-shop vendors' review-request flows (does a 2-star responder get diverted from Google?). Deliver a risk-ranked location report and remediation playbook, then quarterly monitoring and a vendor certification for compliant review-request software.
why_now: Warning letters (Dec 2025), the first orders (July 2026) and law-firm commentary in mid-2026 show an enforcement pattern taking shape, and Italy's Mar 2026 Trustpilot fine shows the referee itself can be penalised.
revenue_model: $5-25k per audit scaled by location count, $2-8k per month monitoring, and certification fees from review-software vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Liability sits with the buyer of reputation software, not the vendor, and those vendors' flows were designed when gating was legal. The money follows the risk to the franchisor's general counsel.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical, either dental support organisations or auto dealer groups. Cold-email 40 general counsel with a free three-location sample audit. Build scanners on public review data and line up two law firms as referral partners.

title: Agent-Bookable Gateway for Local Trades
one_liner: A per-business endpoint that lets consumers' AI agents get a photo-based quote, hold a slot and pay a deposit at a local trade without a phone call.
customer: House cleaners, junk-removal crews, pressure washers, mobile detailers, movers, handymen and groomers (1-15 staff) with weak or template websites.
problem: Consumers increasingly ask assistants to 'find and book' local help. Agents can't get a price, slot or deposit from a local trade without a call, so trades are invisible to agent-driven demand. Reviews and SEO matter less than being machine-readable and bookable.
solution: Each business gets an agent endpoint: photo-to-quote with vision models, service area and rules (minimum job, blackout dates), live slot holds, and a payment link for the deposit. It is exposed through structured data, an OpenAPI or MCP interface, and registered with agent platforms and directories. Owners set guardrails and approve borderline quotes by text.
why_now: Consumer agents and agentic-commerce protocols emerged in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), vision models can price photo-priceable jobs, and 46% of small firms already use AI, so owners are open to the concept.
revenue_model: $49/month plus a 3-5% booking fee on agent-originated jobs.
non_obvious_insight: The next website is a callable endpoint, and the first vertical where agents can close is the one where jobs are priceable from photos. Scheduling incumbents hold the data but may not expose a public agent interface, so a neutral gateway can win a directory position.
first_30_days: Sign 20 operators in two photo-priceable verticals, publish their endpoints and test with the major assistants' agent modes plus manual concierge. Measure agent-originated bookings and quote accuracy.

title: Vaults After Banks
one_liner: Buy or lease closed bank branches with intact vaults and reopen them as private safe-deposit clubs for the people banks are abandoning.
customer: Crypto self-custodians storing seed-phrase backups, families doing estate planning, small collectors and small businesses. Referral channels are estate attorneys and financial advisors. Boxes run $150-900/yr.
problem: Big banks are exiting safe-deposit service. JPMorgan is reported to be leaving the business, and Santander and Capital One have stopped new boxes. Large boxes have multi-year waitlists in cities. Storing seed phrases or a will at home is risky, and a bank box has a known weakness: heirs can't get in without a court process.
solution: Acquire or lease shuttered branches whose UL-rated vaults and box banks are already installed. Sunk-cost vaults are nearly worthless to a seller and costly to build new. Add modern access control (biometrics plus dual-key, video, private viewing booths) and insurance. Build a strong KYC and lawful-process program from day one, without inventorying box contents. Then differentiate with a sealed 'Legacy Envelope': tamper-evident, chain-of-custody logged, and released to named heirs through an attorney-verified protocol. Add a notary and witness room for signing estate documents on site.
why_now: Bank exits are accelerating through 2025-26, and branch closures keep feeding the market with sale-ready vault buildings. Self-custodied crypto has gone mainstream, and holders are worried about physical coercion. Independent operators like BlueVault report growing demand, so the model is proven but far from saturated outside a few metros.
revenue_model: Annual box rent ($120-900 by size). One-time onboarding fee. Legacy Envelope release plans ($60/yr plus $250 on release). Hourly notary and witness room. Attorney and advisor referral fees. A 1,500-box vault at about 70% fill and $300 average is roughly $315k/yr against a building that can cost $250-500k.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust and the legal chain of custody after death, not the steel. Banks leave because a box earns little against corporate overhead, but a one-branch boutique with a lawyer-drafted custody agreement is profitable. The US Private Vaults FBI seizure in 2021 shows the failure mode, so the winning brand is 'privacy plus compliance', never 'no questions asked'.
first_30_days: Pull 20 recently closed branches from LoopNet and bank real-estate-owned lists and shortlist the ones with intact vaults and box banks. Get a vault-contractor inspection and an insurance quote. Have a lawyer draft the custody agreement and Legacy Envelope protocol. Open a waitlist with $100 refundable founding-member deposits, targeting 300 members through crypto meetups and estate-attorney networks before signing a lease.

title: Camera-Free Certified: No-Record Spaces for Smart Glasses
one_liner: A certification, signage, staff-training and radio-detection service that lets gyms, spas, clinics and bars credibly promise 'no recording devices here' as camera glasses go mainstream.
customer: Owners of boutique gyms and pilates studios (especially women-focused), salons and spas, therapist and medical practices, schools, coworking spaces and event organizers. Their insurers are the eventual channel.
problem: Camera glasses look like ordinary eyewear. Researchers and journalists have documented men covertly filming women in gyms, workplaces and beaches. New York State courts banned them from all 1,240 courthouses in July 2026, and the Air Force, DEF CON 34 and UK Comic Con have banned them too. Yet as of July 2026 no major US gym chain had a formal smart-glasses policy, and staff have no acceptable way to check.
solution: Three tiers. (1) A policy kit with signage, member-agreement language and staff scripts ($29-49/month). (2) A 'Camera-Free Certified' badge with mystery audits, listed in a consumer directory of no-record places. (3) A discreet front-desk appliance or app that passively scans for the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals glasses emit and quietly alerts staff. Start with the kit and badge, and add detection once there are customers.
why_now: Smart-glasses sales climbed after Meta's Ray-Ban Display launch in late 2025. In 2026 scandals reached the mainstream, Meta bricked units with tampered recording LEDs, and institutions began banning them in a burst. Venue owners now face the liability question first.
revenue_model: $39-299 per month per venue by tier, plus one-time detection hardware, audit fees, and later insurer referral fees for certified venues.
non_obvious_insight: Bans fail without enforcement, and enforcement fails without a socially acceptable way to check. The moat is the certification norm, like 'smoke-free' or 'kosher', not the detector, which is a commodity. Women-only gyms and studios are the beachhead because 'safe to change here' is a direct marketing hook, and once one studio in a town is certified its competitors have to follow.
first_30_days: Ship the policy kit and printable signage in week one. Pitch 30 boutique studios, spas and therapist offices with a 'be the first certified venue in your city' offer. Aim for 10 paying at about $39/month. Build a Raspberry Pi or phone-based BLE scanning prototype with one pilot studio and launch a simple map of certified spaces.

title: Pre-Dawn Childcare Pods for Construction Crews
one_liner: Contractors buy reserved 5:00am-4:00pm childcare slots near job sites from licensed home providers, so crews can start at 6am without losing parents.
customer: General contractors and specialty subs (electrical, framing, concrete), especially on data-center and big subdivision projects, plus local homebuilder associations and apprenticeship funds. The 45F credit lets them recover 40-50% of the cost.
problem: Crews start at 5:30-7am and often work 10-12 hour days, but licensed care opens at 6:30-7am. ICE enforcement, retirements and data-center overtime are already draining the workforce, and construction is only about 4% women. Providers cannot staff 5am hours without guaranteed revenue. Childcare workers earn about $33K, so nobody can afford premium-hour pay.
solution: Contract with licensed family providers and small centers near job sites and staging areas to run early-hours pods with reserved capacity on a monthly retainer. Cap care at a safe number of hours (about 10) and design for early-arrival sleep. The platform handles enrollment, insurance, shift scheduling, drop-off logistics and 45F paperwork. For megasites with thousands of workers, add factory-built child-care modules on site.
why_now: The 45F credit rose to 40% (50% for small businesses) from 2026 and reportedly allows third-party and pooled arrangements, so a group of subs can share one program. ABC says construction must add 349K workers in 2026, immigrant workers are over 25% of the workforce and are being pulled off sites, and data centers are absorbing about a third of the shortage. Retention is the acute buyer pain.
revenue_model: $350-600 per reserved slot per month paid by contractors, 12-15% platform fee on top of provider pay, and tax-credit advisory fees.
non_obvious_insight: The people who cannot use standard 7-6 childcare are the only buyers who will pay a premium, and construction employers already pay per-diems, housing and overtime to keep skilled hands. Replacing one journeyman costs thousands, so a few hundred dollars a month for a reliable slot is cheap. A retainer is what unlocks provider supply for the early hours.
first_30_days: Choose one metro with a data-center or subdivision surge. Interview 10 subs' HR or safety directors and survey crews on childcare needs. Sign two family providers willing to open at 5am for guaranteed pay. Sell a pilot of 10 reserved slots to one mid-size electrical or framing contractor, then get a CPA to sign off on the 45F treatment.

title: The Unrecorded Room
one_liner: Hourly, certified no-recording rooms (phone lockers, no AI notetakers, analog paper only) for conversations too candid to survive a transcript.
customer: General counsels and outside counsel, boards and special committees, M&A and restructuring teams, VC-founder negotiations, HR investigators, and labor-management negotiators in one dense business district. They pay $200-400/hour or $2-5k/month firm memberships.
problem: AI notetakers now sit in most meetings. In mid-2026 firms such as Mayer Brown were warning that they create discoverable transcripts and privilege risk, and in February 2026 Judge Rakoff (SDNY) held that a defendant's chats with an AI platform were not privileged. Virtual meetings can't be sealed. Even offices are full of transcribing laptops, smart speakers, and phones. Leaders' workaround is 'let's take a walk'.
solution: Rooms with phone and laptop lockers, RF-shielded walls, whiteboards and paper pads, and a sign-in ritual. All attendees sign an 'Unrecorded' attestation that no recording or AI tool is in use. The venue logs who attended, never what was said. It offers concierge booking and a 'war room' day package. Counsel reviews the model so the room never destroys existing records, only avoids creating new ones. Later it certifies hotel suites and law-firm floors as 'Unrecorded Certified'.
why_now: AI notetaker penetration is high, and 2026 legal commentary and case law make the privilege and discovery risk concrete. The person paying is the person personally liable for the record.
revenue_model: Hourly room fees, firm memberships, and day-long war-room packages ($3k). White-label and certification fees from hotels and law-firm floors.
non_obvious_insight: In a fully transcribed world, the provable absence of a record is a premium product, and the buyer is the person with legal liability. Invitation to the unrecorded room becomes a high-trust status marker. It is a venue business that is not competing with coworking, because it sells evidence that nothing was kept.
first_30_days: Lease 3-4 rooms inside an existing coworking or law-office building on revenue share. Give CLE talks at the local bar association on 'AI notetakers and privilege' as a cheap lead engine. Have a TSCM consultant validate a low-cost shielding and locker setup. Pre-sell 10 firm memberships.

title: Church-Basement Microschools for Retired Teachers
one_liner: A turnkey venue, insurance, fire-code and ESA-billing kit that lets a retired teacher open an 8-15 student paid school in a congregation's empty weekday classrooms.
customer: Retired or soon-to-retire teachers aged 55-70 pay a monthly fee and a share of tuition. Congregations are the landlords. Parents are the end payers, through education savings account (ESA) funds.
problem: Microschool builders assume curriculum and tech are the hard part. What actually kills these schools is the certificate of occupancy and zoning, the fire marshal, liability insurance, ESA vendor approval and reimbursement paperwork, and bookkeeping. Retired teachers have the credibility and skills but no business experience. Meanwhile congregations hold Sunday-school classrooms that sit empty Monday to Friday and need rent.
solution: A state-by-state permit packet (occupancy class, what the inspector will actually ask for). A pre-negotiated group liability policy for microschools. A standard five-day lease with congregations covering rent, cleaning, security and safeguarding. Onboarding for ESA and voucher programs (including any accreditation or approved-provider requirements) plus back-office billing and attendance. A menu of curricula so the teacher chooses. A shared bench of substitute retired teachers for sick days.
why_now: Texas launched its Education Freedom Accounts in fall 2026 with $1 billion, about $10,474 per student in 2026-27 (a 12-student school is roughly $125k in revenue), and about 600 private schools and pre-K providers applied in the first 10 days. Universal or near-universal ESAs are live in a growing list of states, and a federal scholarship tax credit begins in 2027. About 1.5 million students are already in microschools, and teacher retirements are climbing.
revenue_model: $199-$399/month platform fee per school, about 4% of tuition processed, insurance commissions, and a 5% lease-admin fee from congregations.
non_obvious_insight: Pension re-employment caps generally bite when you return to a covered public district. Working for yourself in a private school usually does not touch your annuity (verify by state), and past full retirement age the Social Security earnings test no longer applies. So a retired teacher can keep her pension and collect full tuition. Parents' top trust signal is 'Mrs. Alvarez taught 31 years at Lincoln Elementary.' A church building that is already zoned, already inspected for children, and rents for $800-$1,500 a month is the cost moat. Curriculum is commodity. Occupancy and insurance are the moat.
first_30_days: In Texas or Arizona or Florida, recruit a cohort of 10 retired teachers through retired-educator associations and Facebook groups. Line up 5 congregations with weekday space. Build the permit checklist for one city, get one group insurance quote, and sign 3 pilot schools at $299/month. Target the January 2027 semester and the early-2027 ESA application cycle for 2027-28, since fall 2026 enrollment has already closed.

title: SNAP-Ready Kits for Corner Stores
one_liner: A UPC-level 'variety counter' plus a pre-built wholesale fill kit that tells a convenience store exactly what to stock to keep SNAP authorization under USDA's new staple-food rule.
customer: Independent convenience stores, bodegas, small groceries and dollar-format stores that accept SNAP (USDA counts 269,217 authorized retailers, with small-format stores hit hardest). The store owner pays for the audit and kit. Secondary payers are the local cash-and-carry wholesalers and jobbers who earn incremental case sales, and city or state health departments that fund healthy-corner-store programs.
problem: USDA's final rule (effective July 7, 2026; implementation Nov 4, 2026) raises the stocking floor from 3 to 7 varieties in each of 4 staple categories (28 varieties), with 3 stocking units each (84 units) and perishables in 3 categories. The counting rules are counterintuitive: brown and white rice are one variety, all bread is one variety, and brands and flavors do not count. USDA's own analysis of 121,294 small-format stores found only 52% already stock enough dairy varieties and 63% enough protein, which implies roughly 58,000 stores short on dairy alone. Stores are assessed at reauthorization (every 5 years, about 54,000 stores a year) or at any time. Owners have no tool that tells them what to buy, and commenters said the rule is infeasible for small stores.
solution: An SMS and web tool. The owner uploads a POS export or photographs shelves. A classifier maps UPCs to USDA's variety groups, using the rule's Group 1 and Group 2 counting logic, and returns a gap list such as 'need 3 more dairy varieties and 2 more protein varieties, buy these SKUs'. A sold-through kit pre-negotiated with a local wholesaler uses the lowest-spoilage items that fit small refrigeration. The tool also produces a USDA evidence pack (dated photos, invoices, variety ledger) for reauthorization or a compliance review. A 'keep or drop SNAP' ROI calculator is built in, because most small stores earn little from SNAP.
why_now: USDA published the final rule on May 8, 2026 and the enforcement-ready implementation date is Nov 4, 2026, about five weeks out. The prior interim standard was only 3 varieties per category, so almost every small store has a gap to close. USDA also says it can assess any retailer at any time, and every store hits reauthorization within 5 years, so demand arrives as a rolling wave rather than a single date.
revenue_model: $79 one-time shelf audit, or free through wholesaler partners. Kit sold at wholesale plus a 10-15% margin, or a referral fee from the wholesaler. $29 per month monitoring with auto-reorder and evidence-pack refresh. Grant-funded 100-store packages ($500-1,500 per store) sold to health departments and food-access nonprofits. Anonymized gap data licensed to distributors.
non_obvious_insight: USDA admits it has no baseline data on how many stores fail, and its roughly $77M first-year cost estimate describes 'reviewing notice, guidance, and updating stock', which works out to a few hundred dollars per store. That looks far too low against stocking 28 varieties with perishables in tiny coolers, and commenters said so directly: 'refrigerated space is limited for perishable products... would lead to waste and higher operating costs' and 'stocking seven distinct grain varieties... is not feasible for small convenience stores'. Convenience stores are 44% of SNAP retailers but only 5% of redemptions and 76% of sanctions, so many owners will do the math and drop SNAP unless compliance is cheap and certain. The rule also leaves 'perishable' and 'stocking unit' undefined, which creates an interpretation gap that a shared variety ledger can fill. Evidence: final rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/08/2026-09137/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance and proposed rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/25/2025-18624/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance
first_30_days: Pick one metro with dense small-format stores. Sign one cash-and-carry wholesaler or jobber as the kit supplier. Encode the rule's variety-counting logic into a spreadsheet-based counter and walk 40 stores with a $79 audit, aiming for 15 paid audits and 5 kit orders. Publish a one-page 'what counts as a variety' guide and post it in grocer association WhatsApp and Facebook groups. Pitch the local health department a grant-funded 100-store pilot using the audit results as proof.

title: After-School Shop Clubs Run by Retired Tradespeople
one_liner: Screen-free after-school care for ages 10-15 inside idle trade-school and union shops, staffed by retired journeymen who teach kids to build real things.
customer: Parents of 10-15-year-olds paying about $180-260 a month, plus sponsors (contractor associations, distributors, JATCs and local subs) paying $150-300 per enrolled kid as a recruiting pipeline. State child-care subsidy vouchers where the program is licensed.
problem: School-age care from 3 to 6pm is scarce, and Gen Alpha teens fill it with phones and AI companions (72% of US teens have used them) while under-16 social bans leak. Most of the trades labor gap is retirements, and the pipeline is thinner than headlines suggest (the enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage). Community-college and JATC shops sit empty after 3pm. Retired tradespeople lose purpose and have no channel to pass on skills.
solution: Run a licensed or license-exempt (per state rule) after-school program in partner shops. One certified childcare lead plus paid retired journeyman mentors ($25-30/hr from sponsor funds) run projects such as tiny houses, cabinetry, wiring boards and plumbing trees. Phones stay in lockers. Older kids earn micro-credentials (OSHA-10 at 16, NCCER Core) and sponsors get first look. A small local team can run in three shops in year one.
why_now: Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia have under-16 bans, US school phone bans cover 12 states, and parents want credible offline options. ROAD to Housing Act standard plans and manufactured-home reforms are creating build content and demand for skilled set crews. The retirement wave is driving most of the ABC 349K and 456K worker gap.
revenue_model: Tuition $180-260 per child per month, sponsor fees $150-300 per child per month (or lump-sum program sponsorship), subsidy vouchers where eligible, and mentor stipends funded through sponsorship.
non_obvious_insight: The apprenticeship pipeline's real bottleneck is exposure and mentors before age 16, not training seats. Idle shops, retired mentors and parents desperate for screen-free care are three underused assets that pay for each other. A contractor who pays $3K to keep a local kid in the trades over two years is spending less than the cost of one bad hire.
first_30_days: Partner with one community college, ABC or IEC chapter training center. Recruit three retired journeymen and confirm the state licensing exemption (or license a school-age program). Run an 8-week pilot three afternoons a week for 12 kids at $180 a month, with $500 sponsorships from five local subs, and fill the waitlist through local parent Facebook groups.

title: Cinemas and Arcades as Paid Heat Refuges
one_liner: A standby network of independent cinemas, bowling alleys, arcades and LAN centers that counties activate on heat and smoke days and pay per verified visit.
customer: County and city heat or emergency-management offices, starting with one that has a heat-action plan and a live indoor-temperature mandate (LA County, Maryland counties). Landlords of buildings under indoor temperature caps are the second buyer.
problem: Cooling centers are libraries and rec centers with short hours. Seniors, night-shift workers and teens do not go. Cooling is now a legal duty for landlords: Maryland 80F cap since June 2026, LA County 82F from Jan 2027, NYC 78F from 2030 (secondary sources). When a chiller fails, the fallback is hotel rooms at $150+ a night. Meanwhile independent cinemas, bowling alleys and family entertainment centers sit half-empty on weekday afternoons, with HVAC sized for 300 people.
solution: Pre-contract 20-60 venues per county under a standby agreement. A heat trigger (heat index or WBGT threshold) or smoke trigger (AQI above 150) activates them. On activation, venues open a free-entry lane with water, a screening and a quiet room. Outreach goes out by 211, SMS and health-plan lists, and QR or phone check-in creates per-visit proof. The county pays a standby fee plus a per-verified-visit-hour fee. Landlords can buy prepaid outage passes for tenants when their cooling fails.
why_now: Summer 2026 was reported as the hottest US July on record, and the European heatwave death toll shifted political attention. Cooling mandates are arriving on a 2027-2032 phase-in, so demand is scheduled, not random. FEMA's BRIC money was cancelled, court-restored and then closed to applications on Jul 23 2026, so cities need cheap opex solutions rather than built capacity. Venues want non-ticket revenue.
revenue_model: $150-400 standby fee per venue per heat season, plus $8-15 per verified visit-hour paid by the county. The platform keeps about 25%. Landlord outage passes at $10-15 per tenant-day. Venues keep concession sales.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in a heat emergency is not cold air. It is willingness to go somewhere and stay for six hours. Entertainment venues are dwell-time machines that already hold 300 people at 70F with a reason to stay. Paying only for activated days flips cooling centers from capex to opex with zero idle capacity, and smoke days come free because cinemas can run high-grade filtration.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a heat-action plan and a 2027 budget cycle. Sign LOIs from 5-8 owner-operated cinemas, bowling alleys and arcade bars (phone calls, not enterprise sales). Run an unpaid test activation on the next warm spell or smoke day. Write a one-page cost comparison against hotel vouchers and take it to the county emergency office, one Medicaid managed-care plan and 10 property managers.

title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. Sign 5-10 brands on a paid pilot, record their marks, and produce the first product-identification guides. Line up one IP law firm as the enforcement referral partner.

title: Earn-In Equity for Journeymen Buying Trade Shops
one_liner: A platform that turns a retiring HVAC, plumbing or electrical owner and a 25-year-old journeyman into a multi-year vesting buyout with a pre-agreed valuation formula, seller note and SBA-ready paperwork.
customer: Retiring owners of 5-40 employee trade shops (sellers pay) and licensed journeymen or foremen aged 22-35 (buyers), plus SBA lenders that fund the final tranche.
problem: Most trade-business owners plan to retire within years, yet only about half have a succession plan. Selling to private-equity roll-ups strips the local shop, and employees cannot get $1M+ loans with personal guarantees or clear the licensing hurdles. Owners hesitate to leave, and buyers lack a track record that lenders trust.
solution: An 'earn-in': the journeyman converts part of pay, bonus and sweat into equity tranches at a formula price (a multiple of trailing owner earnings with a collar), while the owner keeps a seller note and consulting role. The platform supplies valuation, legal documents, state-by-state license-qualifier planning, a data room from job and dispatch software, and a lender packet. After three to five years it supports the final SBA-financed buyout, monitoring callbacks and margins as an early-warning system.
why_now: An estimated 6 million small-business ownership transitions and up to $5T of enterprise value are expected by 2035, and Gen Z interest in trades and acquisition is rising. Lenders want buyers with operating history, which a staged earn-in builds. Field-service software now produces clean data to underwrite from.
revenue_model: A seller-paid setup fee of $4-$8k, a 1% fee on closed value plus lender referral, and a SaaS charge of $99-$299 per month for tracking tranches and KPIs. Later, a small gap-capital fund.
non_obvious_insight: The successor is already inside the business, and the bottleneck is trust and time, not capital. A formula-based earn-in makes 'when and at what price' knowable on day one, lets owners retire on a schedule, and lets buyers learn to run the shop before taking on debt. It also preserves local reputation better than a roll-up.
first_30_days: Recruit five retiring owners through local supply houses and trade associations. Charge $2,500 for a pilot 'succession blueprint' plus legal docs. Interview 20 journeymen through trade schools and union halls. Partner with an M&A attorney and one SBA lender. Aim for three signed earn-ins by month six.

title: Health-Check Weekends Abroad, Vetted by US Doctors
one_liner: Three- to four-day trips to Korean and Japanese comprehensive screening centers, with a US physician who prepares you before, translates results after, and coordinates follow-up back home.
customer: Americans 45-65 who pay cash for screening: self-employed, pre-Medicare early retirees, high-deductible households. The wedge is Korean-American and Japanese-American families who already fly to visit parents and trust the hospitals; the broader market follows.
problem: US preventive imaging and endoscopy are sold a la carte and priced for insurers: one whole-body MRI can cost $2,500, and an MRI plus CT plus endoscopy plus cardiac workup can run to several thousand dollars out of pocket. Korea and Japan built prevention into national habit, with one-day comprehensive packages (imaging, endoscopy, cardiac, labs) that reportedly cost 40-70% less than equivalent US screening, but US patients cannot navigate the language, the choice of package or the follow-up when they return.
solution: A packaged trip: (1) pre-trip telehealth visit with a US physician who picks an evidence-based subset of tests and avoids overkill; (2) land package with hotel, interpreter and escort at a vetted university hospital health-promotion center, results in days; (3) post-trip visit where the physician turns the translated report into a US action plan and books any follow-up at home. Group departures create cohorts and lower unit costs. Pair with the Workup Cover idea for the tail if a finding appears.
why_now: Consumers have shown in 2025-26 that they will pay $800-$2,500 cash for a single scan, and K-culture has made Korea an aspirational destination for Americans. Korean hospitals run international patient centers and take intermediary partners, and international screening packages are now marketed in English. US screening costs, high deductibles and the coming FDA and Medicare changes for blood-based tests are widening the gap.
revenue_model: Package margin of 15-25% (travel margin plus hospital partner commission where legal), $250 per physician consult (pre and post), and group or employer retreat pricing for early-retiree communities and small businesses. Optional membership for annual return trips.
non_obvious_insight: The right pitch is not 'cheap surgery abroad', which has a bad reputation, but 'join a country where prevention is a national habit'. The unclaimed value is not the discount but de-risking the two ends of the trip: choosing tests that matter and handling the follow-up in the US. The diaspora is the natural wedge because trust, language and family visits already exist.
first_30_days: Contact the international health-screening centers of three Seoul hospitals and agree one standard package and one heart-focused package. Recruit a telehealth-licensed US physician for pre- and post-trip visits. Recruit 20 pilot travelers from Korean-American church and community groups and longevity forums, take $500 deposits for a first group departure four to five months out, and get six seats confirmed. Keep marketing to screening and prevention, not diagnosis or cure.

title: Independent Verifier for LLM Inference Endpoints
one_liner: Continuous black-box testing that proves an API endpoint is serving the advertised model at the advertised precision, with a price-per-verified-quality index.
customer: AI-native companies and enterprises spending $50k+ per month on inference through routers, resellers and open-weights hosts, their procurement teams, and providers who want a 'Verified' badge.
problem: Endpoints can silently swap models, quantise or truncate context. Research on model substitution in LLM APIs (including an IRIS audit paper in July 2026) shows the problem is real, and a frontier lab's April 2026 postmortem acknowledged unadvertised changes that degraded output for weeks. No standard binds a response to a provider and model, so buyers cannot audit.
solution: Always-on probes from multiple regions using statistical fingerprints, random-string tests, tool-call accuracy and long-context recall. Alert on drift, publish a procurement dashboard of verified quality per dollar and a quarterly integrity leaderboard, and issue a 'Verified Endpoint' badge and SLA to providers.
why_now: Router and reseller markets exploded in 2025-26, margin pressure encourages silent quantisation, and agent workloads make small quality cuts expensive at scale. Fresh research gives credible detection methods.
revenue_model: $1-10k per month per buyer (scaled to spend), a share of verified savings, and $5-25k provider certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: This is a market for lemons. A 20% quality cut is invisible per request but material in aggregate, and the auditor's edge is statistical sampling at scale, not access to the provider.
first_30_days: Open-source the probe kit and publish a leaderboard across 30 endpoints serving the same open-weights model. Get five agent startups to run it, then convert to paid monitoring.

title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.

title: Heat-Number Vault for Water-Project Compliance
one_liner: A registry that matches mill test reports to heat numbers for every pipe, valve and hydrant, producing audit-ready domestic-origin binders for SRF water projects and tariff-tier evidence for importers.
customer: Consulting engineers, contractors and waterworks distributors on state revolving fund (SRF) projects, at $1.5-4k per project. Foundries and importers claiming the 10% US-melt duty tier are the second buyer.
problem: SRF-funded water projects need domestic-origin documentation (American Iron and Steel, Build America Buy America). Section 232 duties now hinge on melt-and-pour or smelt-and-cast origin, and CBP is auditing origin. Certificates are PDFs that do not match heat numbers, and reviewers reject packages. Small engineering firms have no tooling.
solution: OCR and match mill test reports to heat numbers and purchase orders. Flag gaps before submittal, generate the compliance binder, and keep a verified-origin record that can be reused for customs and loan disbursement. Add manufacturer-side badges for foundries with clean records.
why_now: Full-customs-value 232 duties began Apr 2026, with 10% for US-melted metal. EPA announced $7.2B in FY2026 SRF funds, and USMCA rules of origin are tightening after the Jul 2026 non-renewal.
revenue_model: Per-project compliance fee ($1.5-4k), subscription for distributors, and a verification fee for foundries.
non_obvious_insight: Water utility procurement already forces the domestic-origin audit trail that tariff and reshoring tools lack, and the same data proves duty tiers. One dataset serves both the reshoring and water markets, and nobody has connected them.
first_30_days: Pitch five small-town engineering firms and two waterworks distributors. Do three projects by hand with a template plus OCR at $1.5k each. Use the misses and rejections to design the matching logic.

title: Inventory Clearinghouse for Game Stores
one_liner: A store-to-store exchange and standing bid desk that converts hobby shops' slow-moving sealed product into cash or swaps for what customers actually want.
customer: Independent local game stores and card shops (several thousand in the US) that must keep buying broadly to hold their Pokemon and Magic allocation, plus small online breakers who buy sealed at a discount.
problem: The story insiders tell is scarcity: allocation cuts, scalpers, sell-outs. But distributors allocate hot product by account history and volume, so stores end up holding lines they cannot move. Wizards is shipping 7 standard sets in 2026, four of them crossovers (TMNT, Marvel, The Hobbit, Star Trek), and ICv2 reports Pokemon flippers melting down. Cash gets trapped in cold SKUs while the hot ones are short.
solution: A web and SMS app where a store lists overstock (photos, case counts) and sees standing bids from a vetted pool of other stores, breakers and wholesalers. It also finds swaps, such as your Marvel cases for my Pokemon boxes at an index price built from public sold data. We hold payment in escrow, consolidate freight, and guarantee a 72-hour bid on the top ~200 SKUs.
why_now: 2026 has the highest Magic set count ever, and Universes Beyond is now half the calendar. The Pokemon flipper meltdown is compressing secondary margins. Tariffs raised landed costs, so dead stock hurts more. Whatnot's commission change hit existing sellers on 21 Sept 2026, so breakers are hunting cheaper sealed supply.
revenue_model: 3-6% fee on cleared trades, a freight-consolidation margin, and $49/month for bid-desk analytics. Later, short-term working-capital advances against listed inventory.
non_obvious_insight: The same distributor system that starves stores of hot product forces them to carry cold product, and neither distributors nor publishers profit from store-to-store liquidity, so nobody has built it. Stores rarely compete with each other across metros, so they will trade. The clearing spread is the business.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 stores in 2-3 adjacent metros through owner Discords and Facebook groups. Run a manual weekly bid sheet on 30 SKUs using a spreadsheet and Stripe. Spend $30k of your own money on 20 cases of the worst-moving product and resell them to online breakers. First fee revenue by week 3.

title: Compliance Co-op for Group-Buy Hobby Hardware
one_liner: A pooled EU compliance desk (CRA incident reporting, EU responsible person, battery/e-waste registrations, SBOM monitoring) that lets one-person keyboard, FPV, synth and LoRa hardware makers keep selling to Europe.
customer: Boutique hardware makers of 1-20 people in enthusiast scenes: custom mechanical keyboards, eurorack/synth modules, FPV drone boards, LoRa/Meshtastic radios, 3D-printer upgrade kits. They sell through group buys, Tindie, Kickstarter and Discord shops, including US and Asian makers shipping into the EU/UK, plus the boutique vendors that resell them.
problem: Per the briefing, the EU Cyber Resilience Act's 24-hour vulnerability/incident reporting duty went live 11 Sep 2026 for products with digital elements, Data Act connected-product design duties began 12 Sep 2026, and full CRA conformity is due 11 Dec 2027 (fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover). Those duties fall on whoever sells the product, and in hobby scenes that is a hobbyist selling a 300-unit run built on open-source firmware (QMK, Betaflight, Klipper, Meshtastic). The CRA's open-source carve-out protects non-commercial projects, not the person selling hardware with the firmware. Stack on the EU General Product Safety Regulation's EU-responsible-person requirement (in force since Dec 2024), radio-equipment cybersecurity rules, and battery and WEEE registrations (battery labelling duties start around Aug 2026, verify), and the makers' choices are to ignore it or stop shipping to the EU. A EUR 5-10k consultancy engagement is impossible on an $80-300 product.
solution: A membership 'compliance-of-record' co-op. Members get: a named EU responsible person and CRA contact of record (professional-indemnity insured); a shared coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure desk with a tested runbook for filing on ENISA's single reporting platform within 24 hours; a CI plug-in that generates SBOMs and watches firmware dependencies (QMK, ChibiOS, ESP-IDF, Zephyr etc.) for exploited CVEs; declaration-of-conformity and technical-file templates by product class; a battery/EPR registration bundle; and a group-buy contract addendum covering delivery windows and customised-goods withdrawal rights. The co-op also acts as liaison to upstream open-source firmware projects and channels 'sponsored security fixes' to them.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live for about 18 days and the Data Act design duties for 17 (per briefing). Market-surveillance sweeps and marketplace delistings typically follow such dates, and marketplaces already delist listings that lack GPSR data. Full conformity lands 11 Dec 2027, so scenes will look for a shared answer during 2026-27, before any vendor has locked the niche.
revenue_model: Annual dues tiered by EU units shipped (about EUR 390/yr up to 500 units, EUR 1,200 up to 5,000, custom above). Per-SKU onboarding fee of EUR 250-750. Optional micro-levy of EUR 0.10-0.25 per unit that funds the incident desk and upstream firmware maintainers. Paid 'CRA sprint' for makers with more than 5 SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators wrote these rules for companies with a compliance department, but the enthusiast hardware economy is thousands of micro-manufacturers who share the same three failure points: firmware dependencies, 24-hour incident reporting, and an EU address. The scalable unit of compliance is the scene or firmware ecosystem, not the individual maker. A co-op that pools the boring 80% and is trusted inside the scene's Discords beats both a law firm and a generic authorised-representative vendor, because reputation in the scene is the distribution channel.
first_30_days: Pick one scene (custom keyboards on QMK/VIA, or LoRa/Meshtastic). Interview 15 makers from group-buy vendor lists. Have a compliance lawyer and a firmware engineer write a one-page '24-hour CRA reporting runbook' and post it free in the scene's Discords, r/MechanicalKeyboards and Geekhack. Sign 10 founding members at about EUR 250 for year one, deliver an incident-reporting drill and a template technical file for one product class, and sell fixed-price single-SKU audits. Cost is two part-time experts plus a simple site, and break-even is roughly 40 members.

title: Shift-Matched Nurse Households Near Hospitals
one_liner: Master-lease three- and four-bedroom units near hospitals and match two single-parent nurses with interlocking shifts and similar-aged kids into one household, so overnight and early-morning care is built into the lease. The hospital pays for placement.
customer: Hospitals and health systems (per-placement or per-retained-nurse fee from recruitment and retention budgets), landlords in lease-up (guaranteed master-lease rent), and nurses (their half of rent).
problem: Single parents spend about 35% of income on childcare and the licensed system barely operates at night or on rotating schedules. Nurses' 12-hour rotating shifts do not fit center hours. Turnover of a bedside RN costs a hospital roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile large units near hospitals sit vacant behind concessions, and middle-income renters' late payments rose from 14.3% to 21.6% in a year.
solution: The platform (backed by the hospital's guarantee) master-leases large units from landlords for 12-24 months, then matches nurses on compatible shift patterns, school zone and child ages, with background checks, a shared household agreement, and an optional paid caregiver pool for overlap gaps. Each household pays about half the rent it would pay alone and has an adult at home when the other is at work. Students, residents and travel nurses can fill spare rooms.
why_now: Concessions of 15-37% and 7% vacancy make landlords eager for a guaranteed 12-24 month lease with a hospital-backed credit. Hospitals face the weakest cost position in years (Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027 hit margins of expansion-state hospitals) and cannot afford travel-nurse premiums. Childcare costs are the top named barrier for early-career nurses.
revenue_model: Hospital fee per placed household (about $300-500 a month, justified by retention), plus a 10-15% spread on master-lease rent and caregiver-payroll fees.
non_obvious_insight: Matching on shift patterns is an algorithmic problem no housing platform solves: two nurses on opposite shifts convert the biggest cost in a household (childcare) into an internal schedule, and a hospital's guarantee turns a risky sublease into a credit-enhanced master lease that landlords will happily take at a discount.
first_30_days: Sign a pilot with one hospital's recruitment team and two landlords near campus. Master-lease two 3BR units and recruit four nurse parents from unit-level staffing forums. Write a household agreement and a safety-screening protocol with a family lawyer. Measure retention and shift coverage at 6 months.

title: Airline-Grade Depot Maintenance for Drone Fleets
one_liner: A swap-based depot and records service that applies airline maintenance discipline to police drone-as-first-responder, ag-spray and utility inspection fleets.
customer: Sheriff's offices and municipal police and fire departments running 5-30 docked drones, agricultural spray operators, and utility and rail inspection contractors. The buyer is the program manager or operations lead, paying per airframe per month.
problem: Drone programs are run by one enthusiastic officer or a few pilots. Flying is the easy part. The real risks are battery cycle counts and swelling, motor and prop wear, firmware drift across a fleet, undocumented crash repairs, and no clear rule for when an aircraft is airworthy enough to dispatch. Aircraft techs recognize all of it: life-limited parts, configuration control, intermittent faults, 'no fault found', and sign-off traceability. Agencies also need records that survive scrutiny in court or after an incident. Manufacturer service plans cover their own hardware only and are mostly warranty repair, not fleet discipline.
solution: A monthly airframe subscription that includes a rotable-style exchange pool. When something fails, we ship an airworthy replacement airframe, gimbal or battery set overnight and take the broken one to our bench, so the program is never down. We keep per-airframe and per-battery records with QR codes, cycle counts and firmware baselines. We run a pre-deployment inspection checklist that acts like a simple minimum-equipment list for dispatch. Records are exported in evidentiary format. Techs staffing the bench are retired or moonlighting A&Ps.
why_now: The 2025 White House drone executive order and the FAA's proposed BVLOS rule (Part 108) point toward large fleets flying beyond visual line of sight, and hundreds of US police and fire departments are standing up drone-as-first-responder programs. Tightening US restrictions on Chinese-made drone equipment mean installed fleets must be kept flying for years while spare parts get scarce, which makes maintenance skill a moat. Mechanic supply is also loosening at the edges as retired A&Ps look for part-time work.
revenue_model: $450-900 per airframe per month for the exchange and records subscription, fixed-fee inspections ($150 per airframe), battery-audit fees, parts margin on refurbished airframes, and later a training and certification product for agency pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Drone programs will relearn every airline lesson, and the money is in configuration control and records, not in flying. A rotable exchange pool beats field repair because the customer's real pain is downtime and liability, not the repair cost. Manufacturers mostly sell to fleets of one brand, but real fleets are multi-vendor, so an independent depot with an airline-style record system has room to win.
first_30_days: Pick one metro and sign three agencies or ag operators to a discounted pilot at $450 per airframe per month. Set up a bench in a rented hangar bay or garage with two part-time A&Ps. Run the record system on Airtable with QR labels, and sell battery-health audits and pre-deployment inspections at fixed prices as the first paid products. Use an airline-style monthly 'fleet status' report as the marketing piece. By day 30, the target is at least one signed agreement and a small exchange pool of two spare airframes.

title: Retired Operators as Fractional Rural Water Chiefs
one_liner: A cooperative of retired licensed water operators, each serving as the certified 'operator in responsible charge' for several tiny water systems remotely plus monthly visits, while converting their tacit knowledge into digital manuals.
customer: Small community water systems under about 3,300 people (councils, water districts, mobile-home park owners, county utilities). State rural water associations and engineering firms refer them. Each pays a $2.5-5k/month retainer.
problem: About a third of the water workforce is eligible to retire within a decade, and tiny systems cannot compete for certified operators. No software fixes 'nobody with a license answers the phone at 2 a.m.' PFAS initial monitoring is due in 2027, the lead action level tightens to 0.010 mg/L on Nov 1, 2027, and nitrate hits small farm-belt systems hardest. Meanwhile 60-72-year-old operators want part-time income, autonomy and purpose.
solution: Recruit retirees holding Grade 2-4 certifications. Each covers 3-5 systems using remote SCADA and camera access, a compliance calendar (sampling, PFAS monitoring, lead-inventory reporting, consumer confidence reports) and a shared on-call rotation inside the co-op. Every operator records an 'exit interview' that becomes site-specific SOPs (which valve sticks, which well drops in August). A young apprentice is attached to each cluster so succession is built in. The co-op keeps 25-30%.
why_now: 2027 PFAS and lead-rule deadlines are close, and $7.2B of FY2026 State Revolving Fund money flows to systems that must show capable operations. Boomer retirements are peaking. Federal technical capacity is shrinking (EPA's research office was eliminated in 2026), and small systems are left on their own.
revenue_model: $2.5-5k per system per month retainer, of which the co-op keeps 25-30% and the operator earns roughly $30-50k a year part-time. One-off compliance projects (PFAS sampling programs, lead service line inventories) add $5-20k each.
non_obvious_insight: Tiny systems do not need 'AI SCADA'. They need one accountable licensed human, and the only growing supply of licensed operators is retirees. Many states let one certified operator be in responsible charge of several small systems (rules vary by state and need checking). The retiree's tacit local knowledge is the real asset being lost.
first_30_days: Partner with the state Rural Water Association and get the drinking-water program's list of systems with operator-certification violations. Recruit 8 retired operators through the association newsletter and conference. Sign 3 systems on 90-day trial retainers.
